Log in here » KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — When Nastya Podorozhnya’s relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms. Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began. But days before Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she rushed back to Ukraine to help her sister and nieces get out. As she returned to Poland alongside an influx of refugees in the war’s first days, she witnessed the outpouring of support from Polish volunteers. But she also spotted a risk: Ukrainian women accepting help from strangers could become vulnerable to human traffickers. Nastya Podorozhnya stands in the kitchen of the shelter which the Martynka non-profit is running in Krakow, Poland, Thursday, July 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Claudia Ciobanu) That was when she decided to found Martynka, a helpline and support group for female Ukrainian refugees escaping gender-based violence. Four years later, she is struggling to keep the organization afloat. Funding for refugee support is drying up, hostility toward Ukrainians is growing, and Poland still lacks a long-term integration strategy. As war fatigue deepens, politicians are increasingly exploiting anti-refugee sentiment for political gain. The shift is being felt by groups such as Martynka. While fundraising was relatively easy in the first months of the war, international donors have since turned their attention to other global crises. Martynka’s shelter, located in an inconspicuous two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow, has hosted more than 100 women and children. Women receive help to escape abusers and access medical care, psychological support, jobs and housing. “It often starts with me having tea in this very kitchen with the women and they tell me what happened to them and I say ‘girl, same,’” Podorozhnya told The Associated Press during an interview in the Krakow shelter, referring to her own experience of a man trying to rape her on a street in Poland in 2016. As Podorozhnya and her colleagues struggle to raise enough money to keep the shelter open, she says calls for donations frequently trigger a torrent of online abuse. “It’s because I’m Ukrainian,” she said. Ukrainian refugees contribute to Poland’s economy Around 3.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in the first weeks of the war, according to the U.N. Poles greeted them at train stations and opened their homes to them, while the government granted refugees access to jobs and social security benefits. The two countries share a long history of brutality at the hands of Russia, and Poland remains a key ally to Ukraine in the war. By the end of 2022, the number of Ukrainian refugees in Poland had stabilized at around 1 million. Those who stayed were rapidly absorbed into the labor market: More than 70% found employment, and a Deloitte study estimated that they contributed 2.7% of Poland’s gross domestic product in 2024. In addition to the refugees, most of whom are women and children, more than 1 million Ukrainians were already living in Poland before the war, primarily as economic migrants. Historical grievances resurface The refugees have increasingly become targets of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric. In research published this year, Ukrainian migrants interviewed by Olena Babakova, a researcher at Warsaw’s Vistula University, identified the 2025 Polish presidential campaign as the period when anti-Ukrainian feeling intensified, as it became a common theme for all parties, not just the far right. Karol Nawrocki, representing the national-conservative camp and who eventually won the presidency, promised legislation that would prioritize Polish citizens over Ukrainians when accessing public services. Rafał Trzaskowski, the liberal candidate, proposed restricting child welfare benefits for Ukrainians. As tensions increased, historical grievances between the countries resurfaced. In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy decided to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during World War II, causing outrage in Poland. Nawrocki responded by withdrawing a state honor awarded to Zelenskyy, further escalating the tensions. “And it’s not only negative feelings, Ukrainians really experience hostile conversations and attacks,” Babakova told the AP. According to data from the Polish police, 180 Ukrainian citizens were victims of prejudice-motivated crimes by mid-July, a significant increase compared with 275 for the whole of 2025 and 267 in 2024. In response to multiple media reports of Ukrainians beaten on Polish streets over the summer, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in late July that “we must wage war on violence and hatred.” Help for vulnerable refugees is decreasing The Polish government has been steadily cutting support for Ukrainian refugees, saying that many have stabilized their situation. Poland’s ombudsman has warned that the changes disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups, including single mothers with several children, older people and those with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Because most Ukrainian men of military age, between 23 and 60, are prohibited from leaving the country, single mothers are overrepresented among the refugees. Yuliia Repenko from the Ukrainian House said that her nongovernmental organization, which provides help to Ukrainians, was “increasingly supporting people who are particularly vulnerable to exclusion.” The Polish government has defended its decision to cut back aid to Ukrainian refugees. Katarzyna Nowakowska, Poland’s deputy minister for family, labor and social policy, told the AP that the most vulnerable applicants still receive direct help from the state and any other refugees needing support should turn to social workers. Sign up for Business Weekly As the Polish government has been scaling back its support, international aid has also declined, further limiting options. Data from the U.N. refugee agency shows a steady drop since 2022 in the funding provided by international donors for Ukrainians, with only half the agency’s identified needs financed this year, compared with 94% in 2022. “Financial supporters have moved on from helping Ukrainian refugees, but the war is still ongoing,” said Sonia Novytska, a Martynka helpline worker. “If anything, it has become deadlier since the start.” Martynka received about 1,800 requests for help last year, and staff expect that number to increase, Novytska said. Not only victims of violence contact the helpline now, but also mothers struggling to provide food and shelter for their children. “What Poles need to understand is that we are helping the people that could otherwise become homeless in their neighborhoods, the people who might start abusing substances out of despair they can’t make ends meet,” Podorozhnya said. “Martynka does the job of the Polish state,” she said. (CNS photo/Paul Haring) Was Pope Benedict XVI an “outlier”? That is the view of Mike Lewis on the liturgical views of Pope Benedict XVI. Writing at “Where Peter Is,” Lewis casts Ratzinger–before, during, and after his pontificate–as an “outlier” in the post-Vatican II liturgical project. According to Lewis, Montini faithfully implemented Vatican II’s liturgical reform vision, Luciani welcomed it, Wojtyła continued it, and Bergoglio and Prevost defend it. Ratzinger is the one allegedly out of step in the liturgical dance. I don’t share that take. For one, I think several threads are tangled up here. Without attributing a motive to Lewis, I think there is a larger drive of historical revisionism under the surface behind this debate. Various circles that want to pretend that Vatican II launched reforms (not just liturgical) which Paul VI–if sometimes with doubts–implemented, but that the reforming spirit of the Council was waylaid for three-some decades while the Church wandered in the desert during the John Paul II/Benedict XVI era, only to have the “true” spirit of Conciliar reform recovered under the leadership of Pope Francis. Proponents of the liturgical status quo are a subset of that larger “reform” crowd, often with their own agenda. Much of which seems to be seeing bogeymen of SSPX-ism in any questioning of what is called “Vatican II liturgy reform” 60 years out. As for the subset of liturgical reform, I want to draw out several distinct themes. First, not everything done in the name of the Council ipso facto means that those things reflect the will of the Council. Much has been done in the Council’s name and, often, even more tenuously, in the name of the “spirit of Vatican II,” whose link to the Council requires suspension of disbelief. Take some issues that have become lightning rods, such as altar rails. Let’s be honest. There is nothing in Sacrosanctum Concilium prescribing altar rail removal. I cannot imagine the average bishop who voted for the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy (such as my then-bishop in Trenton, the relatively traditional George W. Ahr) understanding his “placet” meant churches across the world should proceed to wreckovate their sanctuaries, resulting in the sanctuary bleeding into the rest of the church. It’s perhaps why sanctuaries of German cathedrals are put at the disposal of chicken jugglers while Home Depot parking lots become inviolate “sanctuaries” for illegal aliens. I know there are liturgists who advocated for it in the name of “full and conscious participation of the faithful” participating in “celebrating” the Eucharist. And I know they were able to write the implementing documents that, in many cases, did not prescribe but suggested that possible outcome. Nevertheless, liturgical vandals quickly befell churches, “renewing” them in the name of an interpretation of what the Council required. Yes, it is arguably an interpretation. And, six decades after the Council, asking whether interpretations of the Council have stood the test of time is not a betrayal of the Council, much less a schismatic act that threatens ecclesiastical “unity.” The same can be said, mutatis mutandis, about the ongoing back-and-forth about the placement of the tabernacle. Behind that issue lies another question arguably none of the Council Fathers thought they were ratifying: that focus on the Eucharist as “source and summit” of the Christian life would be taken to mean that the reserved sacrament, the tabernacle, and Eucharistic adoration outside of Mass would acquire at least de facto subordinate places in typical post-Conciliar Catholicism, ostensibly as something their decisions mandated. Compound this with suspicions about what people’s intentions might be, and one arrives at a kind of toxic liturgical “unity.” Consider, for example, the Bishop of Charlotte telling priests in 2025 not to use pre-1969 prayers when putting on vestments (the current Missal provides no vesting prayers ), because it might be assumed to be a throwback to former liturgical forms. Is it better for priests not to pray as they prepare to celebrate Mass and to treat vesting as a purely utilitarian function for donning anachronistic clothing, ecclesiastical cosplay? Is the current banter that characterizes many a sacristy a more fitting pre-Mass atmosphere? All this leads us back to the question of interpretation. Sixty years–three generations after Vatican II—is an appropriate interval by which to make an honest, nonpolemical assessment of the successes and failures of post-Conciliar implementation. That discussion seems to be the sort of thing that faithful Catholics–those who advocate for current models and those who question them–should be able to have synodally and otherwise. It is perhaps the interpretation question where Benedict XVI was really the “outlier.” Pope Paul VI implemented the Council. Lewis pooh-poohs the question of whether Montini truly grasped everything he was “reforming” and whether Annibale Bugnini was not necessarily playing both sides against the middle to get his preferred outcomes. Lewis invokes topline phenomena (“more Scripture, use of the vernacular … and active participation of the faithful”) to argue that John Paul I was totally in line with current trajectories, when the truth is we know almost nothing of where Luciani would have led the Church. Lewis further insists John Paul II was “unambiguous” in his support of new liturgical trends. And he portrays Francis as the one who saved the Church from liturgical regression, a path he sees Leo continuing without engaging “the views of those who reject the reform.” But Benedict, he claims, is the odd man out. I suggest a different reading of history. Paul VI was too close to events to see the full impact of what he approved. Where John Paul I would have gone is conjecture, not history. John Paul II, who authored a book ( Sources of Renewal ) and held regular meetings in the Archdiocese of Kraków on conciliar implementation, also came from a country where many of the liturgical abuses already commonplace in the West were unknown. I suspect he may have discounted some of those reports; I can say from personal experience that, when I would relate to colleagues at the Catholic University of Lublin what was going on liturgically in some corners of the United States, they thought I was exaggerating. There is no doubt, however, that he sought to roll back what he saw as abuses, including the indiscriminate use of extraordinary ministers of the Eucharist, something most bishops failed to back up. Francis, on the other hand, was probably accustomed to freewheeling liturgy in the Society of Jesus and in Latin America, which was in the throes of liberation theology. So Francis was, I think, generally more indulgent of that than of the “rigid” types of which he so disapproved. I cannot predict at this point where Pope Leo is going on liturgy. In that group, Ratzinger stands out. He returned from the Council to see what its improvisational implementation looked like in Germany, especially in the academic milieu in which he lived. Wojtyła’s Church in Poland may have kept the lid on experimental liturgy, but Ratzinger’s in Germany certainly did not—and has not. The German Synodal Church is just its logical outgrowth. For that reason, and as a theologian committed to the Church, Ratzinger did not feel obliged to toe the “company line” about everything being sunshine and roses. He recognized the wheat and the weeds. He properly raised the question, for example, about liturgical translations that ignored the typical editions in favor of the translators’ preferences (and, sometimes, utter creativity). He did not hesitate to invoke the “experience” which is in such contemporary vogue to suggest that some “reform of the reform” was in order. As one familiar with the thought of the great liturgical theologian Romano Guardini–one of the guiding lights of liturgical reform–Ratzinger did not pretend that the perspective of time raised questions about particular things or their consequences done ostensibly in the name of the Council. If that made him an “outlier,” then what Lewis wants is a publicist, not a theological thinker. I say these things in part because I feel a certain kinship to Ratzinger. I would certainly not put myself in his league, but I do share his perspective–one sometimes upsetting to both extremes–that the Novus Ordo was a proper reform that, on balance, has been beneficial for the Church but which, at the same time, is imperfect and, after sixty years, can be honestly assessed for its deficiencies as well as its strengths. That is not a comfortable position for some because it refuses unambiguously to take polemical sides (which should not be a posture in the Church). I recognize that this discussion is burdened by the Lefebvrist rejection of the post-conciliar reforms. But, of course, not every critic of those reforms or their details is a Lefebvrist. Neither is attachment to the Extraordinary Form (which does not include me) a closet subterfuge for Écône and the SSPX. Ratzinger recognized that and was willing to talk about it. If that makes him an “outlier” in some way, it seems more encompassing than the new “inclusivity”. Finally, isn’t it interesting that, amidst all the synodal talk of the past year–including talk that openly questioned received and established doctrine–that liturgical questions have been curiously bracketed out? My apologies if this response seems to sideline some of the contested matters. A simple, elderly lay Catholic (yet with qualifications & a global experience of Christian theology) I’m in joy-filled awe of the perfection of the liturgy of the Holy Mass. In every healthy congregation we begin with a sincere, trinitarian welcome to each other and to our precious celebrant. We then acknowledge that none of us can approach God’s Holiness except by confessing our sins and confidently assuring one another of God’s mercy for all who are truly repentant. We pray: “Lord have mercy, Christ have mercy, Lord have mercy” for our assembled eucharistic community. Then, being newly shriven, we are confident to approach The Throne with loud exclamations of God’s Glory; recalling that Christians began singing ‘Gloria in Excelsis Deo’ before 128 AD! Think of that . . ! The earliest known creed – the old Roman – dates back to about 110 AD and we join together in loudly proclaiming our unchanging Catholic Christian faith in its descendant Nicene or Apostles Creed. This is all a grand and meaningful preparation for our approaching the table of The Lord as shriven, praising, worshipful, orthodox believing Catholics. A body that is truly catholic & thoroughly Christian. That brings us to the place where we can feast on the soul-food of God’s Word: Epistles read and Psalms sung to prepare the way for The Good News of The LORD Jesus Christ Himself, welcomed by our cry of: “Glory to You, O Lord!”. Reverently marking our minds, lips, and hearts with the Cross of Jesus Christ – we’re proclaiming – “We believe – We will tell others – We will forever love Christ’s Word”. How precious it is to listen to the Apostles’ account of Jesus’ teachings & life of miracles that uniquely confront a world in darkness with the Light of the Eternal Truth, in precious texts that come to us from the very start of First Century Christian community, still fresh & vibrant today. Oh! “Praise to You, Lord Jesus Christ!” How often ? do we celebrate The Church as (irrespective of tumultuous politics & discombobulating philosophies & confusticating factions & schisms) THE FAITHFUL PROTECTOR & COMMUNICATOR OF THE 27 HOLY SPIRIT-INSPIRED TEXTS BY 9 APOSTOLIC AUTHORS; the very ‘Magn Carta’ of THE NEW AND BETTER COVENANT BETWEEN GOD AND US. Totally irreplaceable. How wonderful: Catholic Christians have been singing ‘The Sanctus’ from before 96 AD. Shouldn’t we be wrapped in awe as we say or sing this together? Can we sense hosts of holy angels joining in our worship. Jesus, our King, calls us to His table to feed on His Holy Body and drink His Precious Blood; confirming that we have LIFE in Him and He lives in us. Oneness with Christ is our guarantee of eternal life with God & with all those who love God (the whole point of our faith & of The Catholic Church). Hopefully we will all sense our deep unity: graced to be incorporated in One Body, far more that any sense of our individually fulfilling a religious duty! We pray out loud ‘The Our Father’ – given us by Jesus Christ – and express His Peace to all our sisters & brothers. Since every Catholic Christian who has ever lived is eternally incorporate in the One Savior, we are given a very potent reason to persevere in loving & serving each other. This is the love that will demonstrate to the world that Jesus Christ is truly The Son of The Father, given to save us (see, e.g., John 17:23). Sharing Christ’s Holy Flesh that is Real Food, we are together called to His perfect obedience to GOD’s Commandments. Sharing Christ’s Precious Blood that is Real Drink, we are together called to His unshakable, unbreakable, unlimited love. As a passionate human being: incorporation in this amazing Love Feast is highly addictive. As an experienced academic: the logic of the liturgy of Holy Mass is mightily persuasive. There is nothing else like this. What a glorious gift amidst this world of shadows! Quite honestly, for me the magnificence of the Holy Mass renders questions about altar-rails, priestly orientation, the use of Latin, etc., etc., etc. somewhat irrelevant – to say the least. Reply Hmmm, yeah, well, except it’s not irrelevant, as the many centuries of Church history and the writings of the Great Saints clearly tell us. Reply Thanks, dear Mark. Please be specific about the matters at point. Also, of course,, none of the ‘Great Saints’ you mention were free from sin; and, scandalously, The Church, too, has been far from sinless. Even Saint Peter, our first pope, was capable of serious error (Matthew 16:23). None of us, in our right mind, would pit those serious failures against The Master Jesus’ plan for The Church (e.g., see: John 17:20-23). Saint Paul makes Christ’s way plain: “I do appeal to you, brothers, for the sake of our LORD Jesus Christ, to make up the differences between you, and instead of disagreeing among yourselves, to be united again in belief and practice.” 1 Corinthians 1:10. “Let everything you do be done in love.” 1 Corinthians 16:14. Surely needed by The Kerygmatic Church today, in guiding us away from numerous petty, estranging distinctives; even much more that when St Paul penned it. On 9 September 2026, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, hosted Anita Orbán, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Hungary, who was visiting Latvia for the first time. The Ministers discussed bilateral cooperation, European security, support for Ukraine and increasing sanctions pressure on Russia. Baiba Braže welcomed the new Hungarian government's pro-European and transatlantic course, as well as the decision made on 8 September to expel ten Russian diplomats. The Ministers agreed that a diplomatic presence must not be used for activities that threaten national security and sovereignty. When discussing Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, Baiba Braže emphasised the need to maintain the European Union's unity and to continue the strict sanctions. In addition to the major sanction packages, regular and targeted restrictions are needed against businesses, technologies, financial schemes and supply chains that help Russia produce weapons. The Ministers also discussed Ukraine's and Moldova's progress towards EU membership. Baiba Braže expressed her gratitude to Hungary for its regular participation in NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission. The Ministers also discussed the upcoming EU Multiannual Financial Framework. As members of the Friends of Cohesion group, Latvia and Hungary share a common interest in maintaining adequate funding for cohesion, agriculture and regional development. Baiba Braže emphasised that the budget must also foresee adequate support for the security of the EU's eastern border. The parties also discussed expanding cooperation in the fields of energy, innovation and green hydrogen.

Photograph: Casa de Salud View image in fullscreen Gisselle Martinez, a current apprentice, receives instruction from Sujey Merino, a former apprentice and current trainer at Casa de Salud. Photograph: Casa de Salud Building power New Mexico The US urgently needs more bilingual healthcare workers. This clinic might have the solution In New Mexico, where a shortage is acute, Casa de Salud trains college and high-school health apprentices who understand the communities they serve Building power is supported by About this content Cecilia Nowell Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “I ’ll be getting a little bit closer to you to put the cuff on,” Gisselle Martinez said, demonstrating how to take a manual blood pressure in a trauma-informed manner. “It might be a little tight. Let me know if you feel any discomfort and I can take it off.” She’s not a doctor or a nurse – at least, not yet – but a 21-year-old college student. Between classes, Martinez works as a bilingual health apprentice at Casa de Salud, a primary care clinic in Albuquerque, New Mexico . On top of taking vitals, Martinez is certified in harm reduction – she can run a needle exchange and give out fentanyl test strips. And she understands how a patient’s trauma and past neglect can show up in an exam room. “My entire life I had to pretty much translate for my parents whenever they would go to the doctor,” said Martinez, whose parents speak Spanish. That responsibility sometimes felt overwhelming, like when she didn’t know how to translate certain medical terms, or when she herself had to go under anesthesia and explain the risks to her parents. Now through Casa’s de Salud’s apprentice program, she is working toward becoming the certified nurse anesthetist she wishes she and her parents had access to. “As a bilingual first-generation student, I aspire to help my community,” she said. While states across the country face a healthcare workforce shortage , the need is particularly high in rural areas and within Spanish-speaking communities; in New Mexico, 32 of its 33 counties face a shortage. Although they make up 20% of the population, Latinos account for only about 6% of the US physician workforce. View image in fullscreen Trainer and former apprentice Edelin De las Casas shows apprentice Miriam Rios how to run an EKG at Casa de Salud. Photograph: Casa de Salud To provide that care, not just for the community, but from the community, Casa de Salud’s year-long apprentice program has trained more than 300 bilingual high school and college students since its founding in 2005. The aim is not only to help students from marginalized backgrounds get into medical programs, but to keep them in the community. At least a third of the students Casa de Salud has tracked have gone into the healthcare field, with more than half of those attending medical school. “You’re more likely to work in a community if you grew up in the community,” said health apprentice program developer Colette Village Center, who is from the Standing Rock Sioux Nation. “We want to see more representation of lower-wealth individuals, under-represented individuals in healthcare, because that saves lives.” Offering ‘bilingual, bicultural’ care Casa de Salud opened in 2004 when a local physician approached a group of promotoras – trusted liaisons between the community and healthcare workers – in Albuquerque’s predominantly Hispanic and Latino South Valley neighborhood. “There were a few of us women who called themselves the promotoras tradicionales , who would do limpias ,” said Lorraine Cordova, one of Casa de Salud’s founders, describing a spiritual cleansing common in the Mexican folk healing tradition of curanderismo that often uses herbs, prayer and intention-setting to process emotional stressors. The group met every few weeks at a gym in the South Valley, where they offered limpias , massage, reiki, accu-detox and other treatments. Seeing the need for connecting culturally grounded caregivers to the healthcare system, Casa de Salud soon after launched its health apprentice program. Alejandra Casarrubias was among the program’s first students. Today she’s a registered nurse, a sexual assault nurse examiner and clinical manager at Casa de Salud. “You don’t only have to be bilingual, but bicultural,” she said, describing the importance of training healthcare providers who understand the communities they serve. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges , “patients from minoritized races tend to fare better with doctors of the same race”, across metrics like infant mortality and compliance with healthcare plans. Casa de Salud provides care to a patient base that is predominantly Spanish-speaking and 80% uninsured. Because of the health apprenticeship’s bilingual requirement, Village Center says 100% of the apprentices are themselves Latino, and many like Martinez are also first-generation college students. She’s thoughtful about recruiting students not only from local colleges, but through the college assistance migrant program, and the nearby high school, where students have historically undergone the same training. “I already knew about Casa de Salud because my family, back in the day, used to use it,” said Sebastian Hernandez, a 19-year-old health apprentice, who’s currently studying biochemistry and film production and hopes to become an internal medicine physician. Photograph: Casa de Salud Many of the clinic’s patients continue to use alternative medicines like those its founding promotoras offered. “A lot of the times when those people go to the doctor, they get disrespected for having those kinds of traditions,” said Village Center, who added that the clinic still tries to teach health apprentices about those practices. When new apprentices arrive at Casa de Salud, they work their way through different stations at the clinic, starting at the front desk, then moving to taking vitals, and ending in the clinic’s lab, where they process tests and learn how to draw blood and run EKGs. While at Casa, apprentices also help with the clinic’s syringe exchange program and learn about its gender-affirming care program. Alongside their formal training, apprentices also participate in workshops about healthcare history and receive mentorship from their peers and alums. Between patient rooms, the clinic also keeps a bookshelf well-stocked with study materials for university entrance exams and a cabinet full of free scrubs. There are also bulletin boards filled with scholarship opportunities, financial aid advice and information about the local university’s pre-med society. “Any type of grad school that I had seen, whether it be CRNA [certified registered nurse anesthetist], PA [physician assistant], MD, medical school, all of them are so competitive to get into, so it’s intimidating,” said Fabian Corral, an alum of the program who’s currently enrolled in school to become a physician assistant. “But when you’re surrounded by other people who also want to do that stuff, it’s encouraging.” Corral and two other students in his Casa apprenticeship class are now enrolled in the same physician assistant program at the University of New Mexico, where they meet for study groups together. They’re among 16 Casa alums who’ve gone to school to become physician assistants, advanced practice providers who are increasingly filling healthcare gaps in rural communities. “I don’t know what my future holds, but if it has to do with serving the community, then I would feel like I made the right choice,” said Corral.
